cells.tense: Present tense — here, with the pen.
cells.verb: tending what hasn't yet chosen its shape — keeping more than one thing alive without forcing any of them
cells.place: in the open ground before anything's been decided
cells.ask: Tell one person what you're keeping open and why, out loud, so the care has a witness — and let the next thing that's finished be allowed to finish, as a completion rather than a loss.
cells.core:
You're keeping several things alive at once and not rushing any of them into a shape. Nothing's decided yet, and you're not treating that as a problem to fix — you're watering what's there and watching for which one leans toward the light. That's steadier than it looks. Most people either grab the first sprout or let the whole bed go dry.

What this is free to feed next is being seen doing it. If one person knew what you're holding open and what it's costing you to hold it, the tending would stop being a private weight — and when one of these finishes, you could let it close with a clear conscience instead of a quiet grief.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping the possibilities alive without forcing one yet.

cells.tense: Future tense — bracing at a future that can't be written in.
cells.verb: tending everything so hard that nothing gets to grow on its own
cells.place: in the open ground before anything's been decided
cells.ask: Pick one of the things you're keeping alive and imagine it all the way grown — sit in what it would feel like finished, really finished — before you touch the rest of the bed again.
cells.core:
You're managing possibilities that haven't even declared themselves. Every option is being fed, protected, kept viable, because somewhere ahead is the day you'll need the one you didn't save — and you're already living there. So nothing gets to simply be a seed. It gets a schedule.

The care is real; the clutch is what's wearing you out. If you let one of these be fully pictured as done — not planned, pictured, felt — the rest of them would stop needing to be kept on life support. Then the holding could go back to what it's for: growth that doesn't exhaust the one doing the growing.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping every option alive, and it's keeping you up.

cells.tense: Past tense — still standing at a door that's already behind you.
cells.verb: letting what could grow go untended
cells.place: in the open ground before anything's been decided
cells.ask: Don't make yourself care about the bed again. Pick one thing you still quietly hope for and keep walking toward it this week, without proof it'll pay — the tending comes back behind the hoping, not ahead of it.
cells.core:
The ground is open and you've stopped looking at it. Somewhere behind you, tending something didn't take, and you're still answering to that — so the possibilities sit there, undecided and unwatered, and you call it waiting. It isn't waiting. It's absence.

The way back isn't to force yourself to care about every seed again; that's the thing that dried up. It's to find the one hope that survived and keep moving toward it anyway. Persistence pulls the care along with it, and what you're tending starts to come up on its own — growth without forcing, holding without exhaustion.
cells.sheetLine: The possibilities are still there. You stopped tending them.

cells.tense: Disowned present — pen down in a room you're already writing.
cells.verb: quietly keeping more than one thing alive on purpose, and calling it drift
cells.place: in the open ground before anything's been decided
cells.ask: Say to one person, plainly, "I'm keeping this open on purpose" — name the intent behind what you've been calling indecision, and let whichever one has finished be released as done, not dropped.
cells.core:
You're already tending this. Several things are staying alive because you're keeping them alive — a check here, a door left ajar there — and you describe it as not having made up your mind. The care is running and the credit is going to chance.

There's a plainer version of this underneath, and it's just saying so: this is deliberate, I chose to hold these, this is what it costs me. Once the intent is spoken, the holding stops being a secret job. Then when one of them is finished, you can let it go as a completion — not because you were too scattered to keep it.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending this on purpose. You call it not deciding.
